publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Pyramidal cell-interneuron interactions underlie hippocampal ripple oscillations

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: which local circuit interactions generate the hippocampal ripple, and which of three long-standing competing models survives a direct test
span.quote: Three classes of models for ripple generation have been proposed. The first postulates that spikes of CA1 pyramidal cells propagate at the rhythm of the ripple both orthodromically and antidromically in an electrically coupled axonal plexus

span.label: whether pyramidal cells, interneuron-interneuron interactions, or pyramidal-interneuron loops set the ripple rhythm in the intact brain
span.quote: Despite the critical role of ripples for information transfer from the hippocampus to the neocortex and for memory consolidation, and their postulated role in epilepsy (“fast ripples”; Bragin et al., 1999 ; Le Van Quyen et al., 2008 ), the local network mechanisms underlying the generation of ripples are not well understood

span.label: shows pyramidal activation is necessary and fast GABA-A inhibition obligatory, that PV activation alone cannot make a ripple but can pace one, and proposes a hybrid PYR-INT-INT model
span.quote: Using multisite optogenetic manipulations in freely behaving rodents, we found that depolarization of a small group of nearby pyramidal cells was sufficient to induce high-frequency oscillations, whereas closed-loop silencing of pyramidal cells or activation of parvalbumin-(PV) or somatostatin-immunoreactive interneurons aborted spontaneously occurring ripples. Focal pharmacological blockade of GABA A receptors abolished ripples. Localized PV inter-neuron activation paced ensemble spiking, and simultaneous induction of high-frequency oscillations at multiple locations resulted in a temporally coherent pattern mediated by phase-locked inter-neuron spiking. These results constrain competing models of ripple generation and indicate that temporally precise local interactions between excitatory and inhibitory neurons support ripple generation in the intact hippocampus.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: These results constrain competing models of ripple generation and indicate that temporally precise local interactions between excitatory and inhibitory neurons support ripple generation in the intact hippocampus.

span.label: hippocampal ripple oscillations
span.quote: High-frequency ripple oscillations, observed most prominently in the hippocampal CA1 pyramidal layer, are associated with memory consolidation.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: We used high-density extracellular recordings coupled with multisite optogenetic manipulations in awake behaving rodents (n = 26 mice; n = 5 rats) and urethane-anesthetized mice (n = 16; Table S1 available online).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Sharp-wave-driven transient excitation of pyramidal cells combines with the pacing supplied by interneuron-interneuron interactions to produce the ripple (PYR-INT-INT hybrid model)
span.quote: We therefore suggest that a hybrid model that includes SPW-induced transient excitation of pyramidal cells, combined with the pacing ability of interneuron interactions ( Figure 1D ; PYR-INT-INT model), can account for all known features of SPW-ripples in vivo and with most in vitro observations.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: CA1 interneuron-interneuron interactions bind multiple independent local ripple oscillators cycle by cycle into one spatially coherent event
span.quote: Thus, in addition to the CA3-generated sweep that induces local oscillations, CA1 interneuron-interneuron interactions are likely responsible for coordinating multiple local ripple events at the temporal resolution of a single cycle and combining them into a spatially coherent event.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Stronger excitation recruits the PV interneuron population more strongly, and that population sets the oscillation frequency, which is why both sharp-wave amplitude and light intensity raise ripple frequency
span.quote: The correlation between SPW amplitude and ripple amplitude and frequency on the one hand and the correlation between light intensity and iHFO amplitude and frequency on the other hand can also be explained by excitation-mediated activation of the frequency-determining PV population.

span.label: depolarising 80-100 nearby pyramidal cells is enough to make a ripple-like oscillation, so the minimal generating network is small
span.quote: At maximum light intensity, as many as 80–100 CA1 PYR were directly illuminated (Experimental Procedures), suggesting that the minimal network that can support ripple generation is small.

span.label: fast GABA-A inhibition is obligatory: blocking it locally abolishes the oscillation entirely
span.quote: The full suppression of local iHFOs following GABA A receptor blockade indicates that PYR-PYR interactions alone ( Figure 1A ) are not sufficient for ripple generation and highlights the critical contribution of fast inhibition.

span.label: PV interneuron activation cannot create a field ripple but does organise spiking into coherent ripple-frequency patterning
span.quote: Thus, although tonic light activation of PV interneurons cannot induce LFP ripples, it can organize neuronal ensemble spiking into coherent ripple-frequency oscillations, consistent with a modified version of an INT-INT-based timing mechanism

span.label: coherence across sites is not volume conduction; it comes from correlated input driving several local oscillators at once
span.quote: Thus, iHFOs generated by threshold single-shank illumination involve a smaller network than typical spontaneous ripples, indicating that the coherence of ripples across multiple sites observed during spontaneous ripples is not a volume-conducted effect but rather an outcome of temporally correlated SPW input to multiple oscillators.

span.label: synchronisation needs only the RISING phase of inhibition to be fast, because each pyramidal cell fires about once per ripple and a different set fires on each cycle
span.quote: It is important to emphasize that for ripple-related synchronization of pyramidal cells, it is sufficient that the rising phase of GABA A -receptor-mediated inhibition is fast, because pyramidal neurons typically spike only once per ripple ( Figure S1D ), and different sets of pyramidal cells fire on subsequent ripple cycles.

span.label: removing inhibition does not simply stop the rhythm - it converts it into a faster, pathological one
span.quote: The selective suppression of iHFOs by PTX was transient (~1 min; Figure 4C ) and was followed by the emergence of higher-frequency, nonphysiological epileptic oscillations (200–300 Hz “fast ripples”)

span.label: In transgenic mice, light may also have activated CA2/CA3 terminals rather than only CA1 pyramidal cells.
span.quote: In transgenic mice we cannot exclude the possibility that terminals of the CA2/CA3 inputs were also activated by light, but the consistent observations in virus-injected wild-type animals indicate that direct activation of CA1 pyramidal cells is the main cause of iHFOs.

span.label: The effect of the induced oscillations on the content and sequence of spiking during natural ripples was not tested.
span.quote: How the optogenetically induced HFOs affect the spike content, incidence, and sequential neuronal activity during native ripples remains to be addressed.

span.label: The pharmacological and some optogenetic experiments were done under urethane anaesthesia.
span.quote: Although the receptor blockade and some optogenetic manipulations were carried out in anesthetized animals, several control experiments suggested that the results apply to the drug-free brain.

span.label: Changes in oscillation amplitude and frequency during long light pulses may be an opsin artefact rather than a network property.
span.quote: Upon prolonged illumination (e.g., 400 ms square pulse), the amplitude of the oscillatory waves waxed and waned, and the frequency decreased ( Figure 2Ad ), although this change can also reflect opsin desensitization ( Lin et al., 2009 ).

span.label: in transgenic animals the light may also have activated CA2/CA3 terminals, addressed by repeating in virus-injected wild-types
span.quote: In transgenic mice we cannot exclude the possibility that terminals of the CA2/CA3 inputs were also activated by light, but the consistent observations in virus-injected wild-type animals indicate that direct activation of CA1 pyramidal cells is the main cause of iHFOs.

span.label: induced oscillations differ from spontaneous ones in mean frequency and in the phase separation between cell types
span.quote: However, differences were also noted, such as a relatively lower mean frequency of iHFOs associated with a relatively larger phase separation between pyramidal cells and interneurons during iHFOs. Such differences might be explained by the activating mechanisms: during spontaneous ripples, INT receive excitatory input from diverse CA3 loci and CA1 pyramidal cells, whereas during iHFOs they are driven only by the local CA1 PYR.

span.label: the waxing and waning under long illumination may be opsin desensitisation rather than a network property
span.quote: Upon prolonged illumination (e.g., 400 ms square pulse), the amplitude of the oscillatory waves waxed and waned, and the frequency decreased ( Figure 2Ad ), although this change can also reflect opsin desensitization

span.label: whether induced oscillations carry the same spike content as native ripples is left open
span.quote: How the optogenetically induced HFOs affect the spike content, incidence, and sequential neuronal activity during native ripples remains to be addressed.

span.label: during the pathological fast ripples single neurons cannot be resolved at all, so that state is measurable only at the field level
span.quote: During the supersynchronous “fast ripples,” action potentials of individual neurons could not be discriminated due to the temporally superimposed spikes of many neurons.

span.label: cell-type-specific activation and silencing, used here to convert a correlative question into an interventional one
span.quote: Testing of these models has been hampered by the correlative nature of most in vivo studies. On the other hand, interpretation of in vitro studies is constrained because many applied drugs are not selective for specific neuron types and can affect both SPW and ripple generation mechanisms, thus limiting separation into specific effects.

span.label: closed-loop feedback: detect the event in real time and perturb it while it is happening
span.quote: In support of a critical role of pyramidal neurons, local PYR silencing terminated the ripple events. Ripple-contingent illumination in CaMKII::Arch mice for 20–50 ms resulted in localized suppression of PYR spiking and ripple power

span.label: spike-train coherence between spatially separated sites as the test of a common timing source
span.quote: To increase the power of detecting second order relations between spike trains, we agglomerated the spikes of all PYR recorded on the same shank (median, 6 PYR; range, 1–33) into “summed PYR” activity and all INT spikes into “summed INT” (median, 2 INT; range, 1–9) and quantified the coherence between the resulting spike trains recorded on different shanks.

span.label: ripple vs fast-gamma: two names for events separated only by frequency and amplitude, which THIS paper merges by fiat into 'ripples' - the boundary is a convention, not a joint
span.quote: Because SPW-associated fast-gamma and ripple events differ only in frequency and amplitude distributions ( Sullivan et al., 2011 ), for simplicity, we will refer to them as ripples.

span.label: fast ripples = NOT a faster kind of ripple but a nonphysiological epileptic oscillation at 200-300 Hz; the name looks like a subtype and the referent is a pathology
span.quote: The selective suppression of iHFOs by PTX was transient (~1 min; Figure 4C ) and was followed by the emergence of higher-frequency, nonphysiological epileptic oscillations (200–300 Hz “fast ripples”)

span.label: iHFO = the optogenetically induced oscillation, deliberately named apart from 'ripple' so that the model is not confused with the thing modelled
span.quote: induced spiking that organized into high-frequency oscillations resembling spontaneous ripples recorded at the same site ( Figure 2Ab , top). We will refer to these artificially generated patterns as induced high-frequency oscillations (iHFOs).

span.label: PYR and INT here are OPTOGENETICALLY tagged, not waveform-guessed: classification uses the light response plus physiological criteria
span.quote: Units were classified as putative PYR or INT on the basis of optogenetic responses and physiological criteria

span.label: summed PYR = all pyramidal spikes on a shank agglomerated into one train; a unit of analysis constructed for statistical power, which nearly triples the coherent fraction
span.quote: During spontaneous ripples, 258/737 (35%) of the summed PYR-summed INT pairs exhibited significant coherence (p < 0.05, Bonferroni-corrected F test; mean ± SEM frequency, 140 ± 2 Hz; data from 21 awake behaving mice and four rats) ( Figure 6B , top). For comparison, when the same analysis was applied to exactly the same spikes yet with the original tagging of single neurons, only 790/6369 (12.4%) of the PYR-INT pairs were coherent

span.label: contradicts → the hypothesis that tonic GABA release facilitates axonally generated spikes in the axon-net model (Traub et al., 2003; Bähner et al., 2011)
span.quote: Our findings question this mechanism, because activation of PV and SOM interneurons, accompanied by presumed increase of released GABA, aborted rather than facilitated spontaneous ripples.

span.label: contradicts → the simple interneuron-interneuron (INT-INT) model of ripple generation
span.quote: Moreover, these results indicate that LFP ripples are not maintained during inter-neuron activation in the absence of increased pyramidal cell activity, at odds with the simple version of the IN-INT model ( Figure 1B ).

span.label: replicates → Ponomarenko et al., 2004; Nguyen et al., 2009; Sullivan et al., 2011 (within-event deceleration of ripple frequency)
span.quote: As reported previously in rats ( Ponomarenko et al., 2004 ; Nguyen et al., 2009 ; Sullivan et al., 2011 ), the frequency of ripples decelerated from the mean peak of ~150 Hz to ~120 Hz ( Figures 2Ab and 2Ac , top, purple lines).

span.label: builds-on → Stark et al., 2012 (diode-probe optical fibres)
span.quote: The optical fibers used (core radius, r 0 = 25 μm; etched to a cone, NA eff = 0.37; Stark et al., 2012 ) were oriented perpendicularly to and ended at a distance of h ≤ 190 μm above the CA1 pyramidal layer (50 μm above the top recording site of a silicon probe shank spanning 140 μm).

span.label: contradicts → the axon-net / gap junction model of ripple generation
span.quote: However, connexin coupling between CA1 pyramidal cells have not been demonstrated, and gap junction blockers often interfere with receptor-mediated inhibition ( Schmitz et al., 2001 ). Electrical coupling between interneurons, mediated by connexin 36 gap junction protein, is well demonstrated ( Gibson et al., 1999 ), yet genetic ablation of connexin 36 does not alter in vivo ripples

span.label: contradicts → the hypothesis that tonic GABA release facilitates axonally generated spikes
span.quote: One hypothesis is that tonic release of GABA can facilitate axonally generated spikes ( Traub et al., 2003 ; Bähner et al., 2011 ). Our findings question this mechanism, because activation of PV and SOM interneurons, accompanied by presumed increase of released GABA, aborted rather than facilitated spontaneous ripples.

span.label: contradicts → the simple interneuron-interneuron model, which predicts interneuron activation alone should suffice
span.quote: Thus, in contrast to PYR activation, which readily generates iHFOs ( Figure 2 ), non-rhythmic activation of PV interneurons cannot induce LFP oscillations, indicating that a simple version of the INT-INT model ( Figure 1B ) cannot account for the generation of LFP ripples.

span.label: contradicts → recurrent collateral excitation as the ripple timer
span.quote: Recurrent excitation by the sparse collaterals of CA1 pyramidal neurons has also been hypothesized as a mechanism for ripple timing ( Memmesheimer 2010 ; Maier et al., 2011 ). Yet, this hypothesis does not explain why ripples in the CA3 region with its rich recurrent network are less expressed and more variable

span.label: critiques → in vitro studies that dismissed inhibition on the strength of KCl-reinstated oscillations
span.quote: However, the KCl-induced oscillations were very fast (>200 Hz) and were coupled with long spike bursts of pyramidal cells, unlike naturally occurring ripples.

span.label: critiques → systemic diazepam evidence for inhibitory pacing, confounded by effects on ripple occurrence and amplitude
span.quote: However, interpretation of this latter in vivo observation is also problematic, because the drugs also reduced the occurrence, amplitude, and duration of ripples.

span.label: reconciles → the interneuron-interneuron and pyramidal-interneuron model families, as a hybrid PYR-INT-INT scheme
span.quote: We therefore suggest that a hybrid model that includes SPW-induced transient excitation of pyramidal cells, combined with the pacing ability of interneuron interactions ( Figure 1D ; PYR-INT-INT model), can account for all known features of SPW-ripples in vivo and with most in vitro observations.

span.label: fast ripples —distinct-from→ ripple
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — CRITERION: 200-300 Hz and nonphysiological/epileptic. The name reads as a subtype of the healthy phenomenon and denotes a pathology
span.quote: The selective suppression of iHFOs by PTX was transient (~1 min; Figure 4C ) and was followed by the emergence of higher-frequency, nonphysiological epileptic oscillations (200–300 Hz “fast ripples”)

span.label: fast gamma —same-as→ ripple
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.6 — the record marks this weak — identity asserted BY FIAT for convenience within this paper - 'for simplicity, we will refer to them as ripples'. True here, not licensed elsewhere
span.quote: Because SPW-associated fast-gamma and ripple events differ only in frequency and amplitude distributions ( Sullivan et al., 2011 ), for simplicity, we will refer to them as ripples.

span.label: iHFOs —contrasted-with→ ripple
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS WHERE THE DRIVE COMES FROM. 'DURING SPONTANEOUS RIPPLES, INT RECEIVE EXCITATORY INPUT FROM DIVERSE CA3 LOCI AND CA1 PYRAMIDAL CELLS, WHEREAS DURING IHFOS THEY ARE DRIVEN ONLY BY THE LOCAL CA1 PYR.' Two events that look alike in the local field are separated by the breadth of their input, which is not visible in the signal being compared - so a study classifying events by waveform is classifying by something other than the mechanism. Q-483. · strength of the relation: 0.8 — the induced oscillation is kept terminologically separate from the spontaneous one, and the paper lists where they diverge
span.quote: However, differences were also noted, such as a relatively lower mean frequency of iHFOs associated with a relatively larger phase separation between pyramidal cells and interneurons during iHFOs. Such differences might be explained by the activating mechanisms: during spontaneous ripples, INT receive excitatory input from diverse CA3 loci and CA1 pyramidal cells, whereas during iHFOs they are driven only by the local CA1 PYR.

span.label: sharp wave —causes→ ripple
span.quote: Sharp waves (SPW) reflect convergent depolarization of CA1 neurons as a consequence of coincident activity at multiple locations in the recurrent excitatory networks of the hippocampal CA3 region

span.label: pyramidal cells —causes→ iHFOs
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — sufficient: 80-100 directly illuminated cells produce the oscillation
span.quote: At maximum light intensity, as many as 80–100 CA1 PYR were directly illuminated (Experimental Procedures), suggesting that the minimal network that can support ripple generation is small.

span.label: GABA A —causes→ iHFOs
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — necessary, shown by abolition under focal blockade - which is also what defeats the axon-net model
span.quote: The full suppression of local iHFOs following GABA A receptor blockade indicates that PYR-PYR interactions alone ( Figure 1A ) are not sufficient for ripple generation and highlights the critical contribution of fast inhibition.

span.label: picrotoxin —causes→ fast ripples
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — removing inhibition does not stop the rhythm, it converts it to the pathological one
span.quote: The selective suppression of iHFOs by PTX was transient (~1 min; Figure 4C ) and was followed by the emergence of higher-frequency, nonphysiological epileptic oscillations (200–300 Hz “fast ripples”)

span.label: PV —is-a→ interneurons
span.quote: While interneuron activation alone (without pyramidal cell activation) could not generate LFP ripples (consistent with modeling studies; Schomburg et al., 2012 ), optogenetic activation of PV interneurons brought about ripple-frequency patterning of interneuron and pyramidal cell spikes, implying that ripple timing can be set by interactions among PV interneurons

span.label: PYR-INT-INT —distinct-from→ INT-INT
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — CRITERION: interneuron activation alone does not induce a field oscillation, so the pacing model needs pyramidal drive added
span.quote: Thus, in contrast to PYR activation, which readily generates iHFOs ( Figure 2 ), non-rhythmic activation of PV interneurons cannot induce LFP oscillations, indicating that a simple version of the INT-INT model ( Figure 1B ) cannot account for the generation of LFP ripples.

span.label: axon-net model —operationalised-as→ connexin 36
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — the model's testable commitment - and ablating the protein leaves ripples unchanged
span.quote: However, connexin coupling between CA1 pyramidal cells have not been demonstrated, and gap junction blockers often interfere with receptor-mediated inhibition ( Schmitz et al., 2001 ). Electrical coupling between interneurons, mediated by connexin 36 gap junction protein, is well demonstrated ( Gibson et al., 1999 ), yet genetic ablation of connexin 36 does not alter in vivo ripples

span.label: coherence —operationalised-as→ summed PYR
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — the analysis unit was constructed to gain power; on the same spikes it changes the coherent fraction from 12.4% to 35%
span.quote: To increase the power of detecting second order relations between spike trains, we agglomerated the spikes of all PYR recorded on the same shank (median, 6 PYR; range, 1–33) into “summed PYR” activity and all INT spikes into “summed INT” (median, 2 INT; range, 1–9) and quantified the coherence between the resulting spike trains recorded on different shanks.

span.label: iHFOs —distinct-from→ volume-conducted
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — distance falloff excludes passive spread as the source of multi-site coherence
span.quote: Thus, iHFOs generated by threshold single-shank illumination involve a smaller network than typical spontaneous ripples, indicating that the coherence of ripples across multiple sites observed during spontaneous ripples is not a volume-conducted effect but rather an outcome of temporally correlated SPW input to multiple oscillators.

span.label: superficial —contrasted-with→ deep
span.quote: While roughly equivalent numbers of neurons were sampled in deep (toward str. oriens; 994 units) and superficial (toward str. radiatum; 1,131 units) sublayers ( Figure 3B ), we found that entrainment to spontaneous ripples was more ubiquitous in superficial PYR than deep PYR (609/954, 64%, versus 478/842, 57%; p < 0.001, Fisher’s exact test) and that superficial PYR had higher peak gain

span.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
span.quote: Compared to single-site illumination, multi-site illumination triggered iHFOs with higher power (p = 0.0015, Wilcoxon’s paired signed-rank test; nine experiments in four freely moving mice) and lower global frequency (p = 0.001) and reduced intersite variability (power: p = 0.03; frequency: p = 0.04; Figure 7C ).

span.label: Mann-Whitney U test
span.quote: Although the overall probability of spiking during an individual ripple event was higher for INT than for PYR (50% versus 9% of the ripple events, p < 0.001, Mann-Whitney U test, 369 INT and 1,864 PYR; 4.8% versus 0.8% of the ripple cycles, p < 0.001) ( Figure S1D ), PYR spiking gain was consistently higher than INT gain during the first half of the ripple (p = 0.003, Bonferroni corrected U test) ( Figure S1B , bottom, red bar).

span.label: chi-squared test
span.quote: While roughly equivalent numbers of neurons were sampled in deep (toward str. oriens; 994 units) and superficial (toward str. radiatum; 1,131 units) sublayers ( Figure 3B ), we found that entrainment to spontaneous ripples was more ubiquitous in superficial PYR than deep PYR (609/954, 64%, versus 478/842, 57%; p < 0.001, Fisher’s exact test) and that superficial PYR had higher peak gain (mean ± SEM. PYR gain, 12.4 ± 0.5 versus 9.2 ± 0.5; p < 0.001, U test) ( Figure S3Ab ).

span.label: rank correlation
span.quote: SPW amplitude was positively correlated with spontaneous ripple power (median rank correlation, 0.39; p < 0.001; 26 sessions in four freely moving mice equipped with 32-site linear probes) and frequency (0.33; p < 0.001; Figure 2B ).

span.label: circular correlation
span.quote: However, on a unit-by-unit basis, spike phases during iHFOs and spontaneous ripples were correlated (circular-circular correlation: PYR, 0.7, p < 0.001; INT: 0.42, p = 0.009, χ 2 test).

span.label: circular-linear correlation
span.quote: Superficial PYR and INT spiked earlier than deep cells during the ripple cycle (circular-linear correlation, 254 INT: 0.16, p = 0.01, χ 2 test; 1105 PYR, 0.12, p < 0.001; circular-linear model: Φ(PYR) = 2π(0.44+0.55•d)) ( Figure 3B ).

span.label: Rayleigh test
span.quote: Units recorded on the illuminated shank increased their firing rate (37 INT and 268 PYR from four freely moving mice; p < 0.001, Wilcoxon’s signed-rank test, unity gain null) ( Figure 7Da ) and were phase-locked (p < 0.05, Rayleigh test) to the iHFOs (p < 0.001, exact Binomial post hoc test; Figure 7Db ), whereas PYR recorded on nonilluminated shanks were rarely phase-locked (p > 0.05; Figure 7Db ).

span.label: F-test with Bonferroni correction
span.quote: During spontaneous ripples, 258/737 (35%) of the summed PYR-summed INT pairs exhibited significant coherence (p < 0.05, Bonferroni-corrected F test; mean ± SEM frequency, 140 ± 2 Hz; data from 21 awake behaving mice and four rats) ( Figure 6B , top).

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: The mean and SD were computed from the power of the clipped signal during SWS (defined as non-theta, non-movement periods) in the absence of light stimulation.

span.label: Wilcoxon's paired signed-rank test
span.quote: Following focal infusion of the GABA A receptor blocker picrotoxin (PTX) (1 mM in PBS; 13–52 nl, 26 nl/s), iHFOs were abolished on the shank closest to the pipette

span.label: Mann-Whitney U test
span.quote: Thus, intact activity of a small network of pyramidal cells is necessary for the generation and maintenance of spontaneous local ripples, and silencing pyramidal cells either directly or indirectly via interneuron-mediated inhibition aborts spontaneous ripples. Moreover, these results indicate that LFP ripples are not maintained during inter-neuron activation in the absence of increased pyramidal cell activity, at odds with the simple version of the IN-INT model

span.label: coherence
span.quote: To increase the power of detecting second order relations between spike trains, we agglomerated the spikes of all PYR recorded on the same shank (median, 6 PYR; range, 1–33) into “summed PYR” activity and all INT spikes into “summed INT” (median, 2 INT; range, 1–9) and quantified the coherence between the resulting spike trains recorded on different shanks.

span.label: rank correlation
span.quote: Thus, iHFOs generated by threshold single-shank illumination involve a smaller network than typical spontaneous ripples, indicating that the coherence of ripples across multiple sites observed during spontaneous ripples is not a volume-conducted effect but rather an outcome of temporally correlated SPW input to multiple oscillators.

span.label: Optogenetically depolarizing a small local group of CA1 pyramidal cells was enough to generate ripple-frequency oscillations, while silencing pyramidal cells directly or indirectly (by driving PV or somatostatin interneurons) terminated ripples that were already underway.
span.quote: Using multisite optogenetic manipulations in freely behaving rodents, we found that depolarization of a small group of nearby pyramidal cells was sufficient to induce high-frequency oscillations, whereas closed-loop silencing of pyramidal cells or activation of parvalbumin-(PV) or somatostatin-immunoreactive interneurons aborted spontaneously occurring ripples.

span.label: Focal blockade of GABA-A receptors completely abolished locally induced high-frequency oscillations, showing that pyramidal-pyramidal interactions by themselves cannot produce ripples and that fast inhibition is required.
span.quote: The full suppression of local iHFOs following GABA A receptor blockade indicates that PYR-PYR interactions alone ( Figure 1A ) are not sufficient for ripple generation and highlights the critical contribution of fast inhibition.

span.label: Driving PV interneurons alone, even at very high light intensities, never produced a field-potential ripple, which rules out the simple interneuron-interneuron model as the source of the LFP oscillation.
span.quote: Thus, in contrast to PYR activation, which readily generates iHFOs ( Figure 2 ), non-rhythmic activation of PV interneurons cannot induce LFP oscillations, indicating that a simple version of the INT-INT model ( Figure 1B ) cannot account for the generation of LFP ripples.

span.label: Although PV activation produced no field ripple, it did impose ripple-frequency coherence on ensemble spiking, so interneuron-interneuron interactions can set the timing even when they cannot create the oscillation.
span.quote: Thus, although tonic light activation of PV interneurons cannot induce LFP ripples, it can organize neuronal ensemble spiking into coherent ripple-frequency oscillations, consistent with a modified version of an INT-INT-based timing mechanism ( Figure 1D ).

span.label: Blocking fast inhibition reduced the phase coherence between simultaneously induced oscillations at separate sites, showing that interneurons are what keeps spatially separate ripple oscillators locked together.
span.quote: Furthermore, the high iHFO coherence between simultaneously activated loci is reduced by blocking fast inhibition, indicating that interneurons are critical for maintaining spatial coherence of ripples ( Traub et al., 1996 ).

span.label: Pyramidal cells fired roughly a quarter-cycle (about 90 degrees) ahead of interneurons on every ripple cycle, with mean phases of 157 degrees for pyramidal cells and 242 degrees for interneurons.
span.quote: Spikes of CA1 units were phase-locked to the ripple cycles (PYR: 1105/1864, 59%; INT: 254/369, 69%), and PYR spiked about 90° earlier than INT (mean ± SEM phases: PYR, 157° ± 1°; INT, 242° ± 4°; 0° corresponds to an LFP peak) ( Figure S3Aa ) on every ripple cycle ( Figure 3A ).

span.label: Superficial CA1 pyramidal cells were entrained to ripples more often (64% versus 57%) and with higher peak firing gain (12.4 versus 9.2) than deep pyramidal cells.
span.quote: While roughly equivalent numbers of neurons were sampled in deep (toward str. oriens; 994 units) and superficial (toward str. radiatum; 1,131 units) sublayers ( Figure 3B ), we found that entrainment to spontaneous ripples was more ubiquitous in superficial PYR than deep PYR (609/954, 64%, versus 478/842, 57%; p < 0.001, Fisher’s exact test) and that superficial PYR had higher peak gain (mean ± SEM. PYR gain, 12.4 ± 0.5 versus 9.2 ± 0.5; p < 0.001, U test) ( Figure S3Ab ).

span.label: Physiological ripples and pathological "fast ripples" are produced by different mechanisms, because removing fast inhibition destroys the first while creating the second.
span.quote: Our experiments demonstrate that physiological ripples and “fast ripples” arise from different mechanisms, since loss of fast inhibition disrupts the first and induces the latter.

span.label: Locally induced oscillations fell to 2% of local power just 400 micrometres away and to baseline beyond that, whereas spontaneous ripples retained 89% of their power at 400 micrometres, so ripple coherence across sites is not volume conduction.
span.quote: Two shanks away (400 μm), oscillation power was 2% ± 0.3% of the local power (mean ±SEM; 14 experiments in nine mice; p < 0.001, Wilcoxon’s signed-rank test with a zero-power null) ( Figure 7B ), while >400 μm away, induced power was indistinguishable from baseline (0.3% ± 0.1%; p > 0.05).

span.label: depolarising a small local group of pyramidal cells is sufficient to induce a ripple-like oscillation
span.quote: Our principal findings are as follows: (1) activation of a small group of pyramidal cells is sufficient to generate iHFOs. (2) Fast GABA A -mediated inhibition is critical for the generation of iHFOs. (3) Pyramidal cell activity is critical for the maintenance of ripples. (4) PV interneurons can pace spiking in local populations. (5) Multisite activation induces temporally coherent ripples mediated by phase-locked interneuron spiking. These findings are consistent with a model of ripple generation based on PYR-INT-INT interactions

span.label: focal GABA-A blockade abolishes the induced oscillation completely, so pyramidal-pyramidal interaction alone cannot generate it
span.quote: The full suppression of local iHFOs following GABA A receptor blockade indicates that PYR-PYR interactions alone ( Figure 1A ) are not sufficient for ripple generation and highlights the critical contribution of fast inhibition.

span.label: silencing pyramidal cells, directly or via PV or SOM interneurons, aborts ongoing spontaneous ripples
span.quote: Thus, intact activity of a small network of pyramidal cells is necessary for the generation and maintenance of spontaneous local ripples, and silencing pyramidal cells either directly or indirectly via interneuron-mediated inhibition aborts spontaneous ripples. Moreover, these results indicate that LFP ripples are not maintained during inter-neuron activation in the absence of increased pyramidal cell activity, at odds with the simple version of the IN-INT model

span.label: PV activation alone produces no field oscillation even at 100 mW/mm2, but does impose coherent ripple-frequency spiking
span.quote: Thus, although tonic light activation of PV interneurons cannot induce LFP ripples, it can organize neuronal ensemble spiking into coherent ripple-frequency oscillations, consistent with a modified version of an INT-INT-based timing mechanism

span.label: simultaneous multisite induction produces coherence at distances where single-site induction gives chance
span.quote: Coherence between distant sites (>400 μm separation) during single-shank illumination was at chance level, whereas simultaneous stimulation generated intersite coherence similar to that observed during spontaneous ripples

span.label: removing inhibition converts the physiological rhythm into 200-300 Hz epileptic fast ripples
span.quote: The selective suppression of iHFOs by PTX was transient (~1 min; Figure 4C ) and was followed by the emergence of higher-frequency, nonphysiological epileptic oscillations (200–300 Hz “fast ripples”)

span.label: the same spikes give 12.4% coherent pairs as single units and 35% when agglomerated per shank

For comparison, when the same analysis was applied to exactly the same spikes yet with the original tagging of single neurons, only 790/6369 (12.4%) of the PYR-INT pairs were coherent

span.label: connexin 36 ablation does not alter in vivo ripples, and pyramidal-pyramidal connexin coupling was never demonstrated
span.quote: However, connexin coupling between CA1 pyramidal cells have not been demonstrated, and gap junction blockers often interfere with receptor-mediated inhibition ( Schmitz et al., 2001 ). Electrical coupling between interneurons, mediated by connexin 36 gap junction protein, is well demonstrated ( Gibson et al., 1999 ), yet genetic ablation of connexin 36 does not alter in vivo ripples

span.label: superficial pyramidal cells are entrained more often and more strongly than deep ones

span.label: the same induction works in dentate gyrus and in layer 5 of somatosensory cortex, so the mechanism is not hippocampus-specific
span.quote: Selective optogenetic activation of excitatory cells could also induce HFOs in dentate regions and in layer 5 of the somatosensory cortex (n = 2 rats and n = 4 CaMKII::ChR2 mice) ( Figure S3Ca ), and concurrent activation of excitatory cells and inter-neurons generated iHFOs in both CA1 and dentate regions (n = 3 CAG::ChR2 rats) ( Figure S3Cb ). These findings indicate that iHFOs can be evoked in various cortical networks as long as local excitatory cells are sufficiently activated

span.label: induced high-frequency oscillations (iHFOs)
span.quote: We will refer to these artificially generated patterns as induced high-frequency oscillations (iHFOs).

span.label: gain (firing-rate gain during ripples)
span.quote: During spontaneous ripple events, CA1 neurons increased their firing rate approximately 6-fold (relative to no-ripple epochs, “gain”; Figures S1B and S1C ).

span.label: threshold light intensity
span.quote: For quantification of iHFOs, we defined a “threshold” light intensity in each experiment as the lowest intensity that generated iHFOs with comparable (equal to or higher) power to spontaneous ripples.

span.label: summed PYR / summed INT activity
span.quote: To increase the power of detecting second order relations between spike trains, we agglomerated the spikes of all PYR recorded on the same shank (median, 6 PYR; range, 1–33) into “summed PYR” activity and all INT spikes into “summed INT” (median, 2 INT; range, 1–9) and quantified the coherence between the resulting spike trains recorded on different shanks.

span.label: ripple (online closed-loop detection criterion)
span.quote: Ripples were defined as events with RMS2 exceeding three times RMS1 (range, 3–3.5) for at least 8 ms.

span.label: sharp wave
span.quote: Sharp waves (SPW) reflect convergent depolarization of CA1 neurons as a consequence of coincident activity at multiple locations in the recurrent excitatory networks of the hippocampal CA3 region

span.label: iHFOs
span.quote: induced spiking that organized into high-frequency oscillations resembling spontaneous ripples recorded at the same site ( Figure 2Ab , top). We will refer to these artificially generated patterns as induced high-frequency oscillations (iHFOs).

span.label: axon-net model
span.quote: Three classes of models for ripple generation have been proposed. The first postulates that spikes of CA1 pyramidal cells propagate at the rhythm of the ripple both orthodromically and antidromically in an electrically coupled axonal plexus

span.label: INT-INT
span.quote: According to the second class of models, SPW-associated depolarization excites perisomatic-targeting interneurons that, due to the synaptic time constants of reciprocal inhibition, co-oscillate at ripple frequency and generate periodic inhibition that entrains the population of pyramidal cells

span.label: PYR-INT loop
span.quote: In the third class of models, the fast rhythm is generated by short-lived interactions between interneurons and pyramidal cells rather than by the interactions among interneurons

span.label: PYR-INT-INT
span.quote: We therefore suggest that a hybrid model that includes SPW-induced transient excitation of pyramidal cells, combined with the pacing ability of interneuron interactions ( Figure 1D ; PYR-INT-INT model), can account for all known features of SPW-ripples in vivo and with most in vitro observations.

span.label: summed PYR

span.label: optogenetic light intensity applied to CA1
span.term: optogenetic light intensity applied to CA1
span.quote: At low light intensities, the mean frequency of the iHFO was typically lower than the frequency of same-site ripples, but increasing light intensity (for example, 50 ms square pulses, 0.01–1 mW/mm 2 at the center of the CA1 pyramidal cell layer) ( Figure 2Ca ) enhanced iHFO power (median rank correlation, 1; p = 0.002, Wilcoxon’s paired signed-rank test; n = 10 experiments in four freely moving CaMKII::ChR2 mice) and frequency (median rank correlation, 1; p = 0.002) ( Figure 2Cb ).

span.label: single-site versus simultaneous multi-site illumination
span.quote: To examine whether multiple iHFOs are coupled, we illuminated all shanks simultaneously, keeping all other parameters identical to the sequential (single-site) stimulation ( Figure 7Aa ).

span.label: oscillation power and frequency of the induced high-frequency oscillation

span.quote: Compared to single-site illumination, multi-site illumination triggered iHFOs with higher power (p = 0.0015, Wilcoxon’s paired signed-rank test; nine experiments in four freely moving mice) and lower global frequency (p = 0.001) and reduced intersite variability (power: p = 0.03; frequency: p = 0.04; Figure 7C ).

span.label: ripple-band coherence between recording sites

span.label: light intensity

span.label: distance
span.quote: Thus, iHFOs generated by threshold single-shank illumination involve a smaller network than typical spontaneous ripples, indicating that the coherence of ripples across multiple sites observed during spontaneous ripples is not a volume-conducted effect but rather an outcome of temporally correlated SPW input to multiple oscillators.
